item.title: 1 Rider Dies and Several Others Are Injured on a Georgia Roller Coaster
item.description:
One rider died and several others were injured on Monday on a roller coaster at Six Flags Over Georgia, the police said.

The Cobb County Police Department said in a statement that the episode happened at 3:58 p.m. at the amusement park in Austell, Ga., about 17 miles west of Atlanta.

Details about how the rider died, as well as the number of people injured and their conditions, were not immediately available.

A Six Flags representative said in a statement that park officials and the local authorities had responded immediately, but declined to describe what happened, citing the family’s privacy.

“We are deeply saddened by the guest incident at our park today,” the representative said. “Our thoughts and heartfelt condolences are with the guest’s family, friends and loved ones.”

The representative also declined to say which roller coaster was involved.

Christina Morales contributed reporting.

This is a developing story. Check back for updates.

item.title: ‘Girls’ to Return for a Limited Run
item.description:
The voice of a generation — or at least a voice of a generation — is not finished quite yet.

In a surprise announcement, HBO said on Tuesday that “Girls,” the 2010s comedy about millennials from Lena Dunham, would return for a five-episode run. The network did not specify when the new episodes would air or stream, but said filming would begin next year, a decade since the show went off the air.

Ms. Dunham, the creator and star of the show, who is now 40, will return as Hannah Horvath, that aspiring generational voice, along with Allison Williams (Marnie), Jemima Kirke (Jessa), Zosia Mamet (Shoshanna) and Andrew Rannells (Elijah).

“I’ve missed these characters, but for a long time I couldn’t quite picture them in the present day,” Ms. Dunham said in a statement. “Then, right around my 40th birthday, they started talking to me in the shower. And, as you may remember, once this fivesome starts talking it’s pretty hard to get them to stop.”

Judd Apatow, who was critical to getting the show on the air at HBO, will return as an executive producer.

There were, however, some notable omissions from HBO’s announcement. Neither Adam Driver, who played Ms. Dunham’s on-again, off-again love interest in the show, nor Jenni Konner, the co-showrunner with Ms. Dunham during its original run, was mentioned.

In her recently published memoir, “Famesick,” Ms. Dunham describes difficult working relationships with Ms. Konner and Mr. Driver. Ms. Dunham split professionally from Ms. Konner in 2018.

HBO has been no stranger to reviving older comedies in recent years, sometimes without former cast members. In 2021, HBO premiered “And Just Like That…,” a “Sex and the City” spinoff that reunited several original cast members but did not include Kim Cattrall, the actress who played Samantha and who refused to return. “And Just Like That…” lasted three seasons.

During its six-season run, “Girls” never fared that well in the ratings, generally averaging under a million live and same-day viewers. But it frequently kicked off scores of think pieces and essays in national publications and Tumblr posts. Many younger viewers also discovered the show in recent years, a fact that HBO executives have been aware of.

In a video posted on YouTube on Tuesday announcing the return of the show, Ms. Dunham looks at her four castmates during a video call and raises a question.

“Can we still call it ‘Girls’?” she asks. “Because we’re like old as —” before the video of Ms. Dunham cuts off and title card for the show appears.

item.title: Lawyer for Fed Governor Cook Denounces Trump’s New Investigation
item.description:
Lisa D. Cook on Tuesday challenged President Trump’s latest attempt to remove her from her role as a Federal Reserve governor, questioning the objectivity of a White House investigation into unproven allegations that she committed mortgage fraud.

In a letter to the White House viewed by The New York Times, Ms. Cook’s lawyer, Abbe Lowell, said the governor would not be able to attend a hearing scheduled for Nov. 5 because she would be fulfilling her duties in Europe “at financial and monetary policy meetings.”

Mr. Lowell said the earliest that any hearing could take place was after the Fed’s policy meeting scheduled for Dec. 8-9.

Mr. Lowell also questioned the impartiality of the investigation, which will be run by a committee that is staffed with Mr. Trump’s political appointees, including Kevin Hassett, the director of the National Economic Council; Keith Sonderling, the Labor secretary who is serving as acting director of a government ethics office; and Andrea Lucas, the chair of the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission.

“We have significant concerns regarding the objectivity and fitness of the committee for its assigned purpose,” Mr. Lowell said.

Mr. Trump, who has long sought more control over the central bank in a bid to lower borrowing costs, has signaled how he expects the committee to rule. When asked on Friday about the investigation into Ms. Cook, the president called her “dishonest” and said that if the committee found that there was cause to remove her, he would “absolutely” fire her.

“A hearing with demonstrably biased members, unspecified additional allegations, and an unclear schedule for the disclosure of any additional evidence — with no explanation for why it was not previously produced — is not a process that respects the appearance or history of independence,” Mr. Lowell said.

A White House spokesman, Matthew Middleton, said in a statement that Mr. Trump was “performing his constitutional duty in evaluating Lisa Cook’s conduct and eligibility to continue serving as a governor on the Federal Reserve.”

“The Constitution charges the president with ensuring that the laws are faithfully executed and that the conduct of members of the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System is above reproach,” he said.

Mr. Trump’s decision to create a committee comes on the heels of a Supreme Court ruling that denied the president the right to fire Ms. Cook after his initial attempt in August 2025. The justices in June ruled 5 to 4 in favor of Ms. Cook remaining in her job while litigation progressed, but they shied away from engaging in the substance of the claims against her and focused instead on procedural issues.

Mr. Trump quickly seized on that opening, announcing immediately after the Supreme Court ruling that he would continue his campaign against Ms. Cook, who has denied any wrongdoing and has not been charged with a crime despite the allegations being more than a year old.

On the surface, the investigation into Ms. Cook appears to comply with the Supreme Court’s demands that the Trump administration provide the Fed governor ample opportunity to respond and defend herself before proceeding with her ouster.

In a memo dated Oct. 7, the White House stipulated the scope of the investigation, detailed who from the administration would staff it, and declared deadlines for Ms. Cook to submit supporting documents and written statements. It also summoned her to attend the in-person hearing, warning that this could include questioning from Department of Justice personnel.

“The president is going beyond what the Supreme Court required by offering Lisa Cook an in-person hearing that will be conducted in a fair and open process,” said Mr. Middleton, the White House spokesman.

Christina Skinner, who recently stepped down as an official at the Treasury Department and is now back at the University of Pennsylvania as a professor, described the process as “robust,” noting that the president pulled in people from “different facets of the White House ecosystem,” while also giving Ms. Cook “several avenues” to respond.

But for Ms. Cook’s lawyers, the current setup falls far short.

One of their primary concerns centers on the people who Mr. Trump tapped for the committee.

Mr. Hassett, the president’s top economic adviser, has joined with Mr. Trump in frequent criticism of the Fed, which he recently faulted for an “unusually partisan” board after it chose to raise interest rates to control inflation, rather than cut them as the president has demanded.

He had been among the finalists to lead the central bank under Mr. Trump, but the president opted to keep Mr. Hassett in his current post because he viewed him as a reliable, vocal advocate for his agenda.

In the weeks after the administration first accused Ms. Cook of engaging in mortgage fraud, Mr. Hassett defended the power of the president to fire a Fed governor if he determines there is cause to do so. Last fall, Mr. Hassett describing the allegations against Ms. Cook as “serious” and called on Ms. Cook to take a leave of absence until they were resolved.

“The fact she’s not doing that now suggests she’s being partisan,” Mr. Hassett told reporters.

In his letter, Mr. Lowell pointed to past comments made by Mr. Hassett, noting that he “already has publicly insinuated that the President has ‘cause’ to fire Governor Cook.”

Mr. Sonderling, for his part, had previously endorsed Mr. Trump’s views on interest rates, echoing to CNBC recently that the Fed “should cut interest rates.” The Fed’s decision to raise rates came amid stubborn inflation that has exceeded the central bank’s 2 percent target for nearly six years.

Ms. Lucas has carried out Mr. Trump’s agenda at the E.E.O.C., chiefly by undoing what she has described as aggressive attempts by liberals to pursue diversity, equity and inclusion policies in the workplace. She has particularly focused on corporate discrimination against white male workers.

item.title: Bank of America Pays $1.8 Billion Fine for Lax Money-Laundering Oversight
item.description:
Bank of America on Tuesday was fined $1.8 billion, a near-record, for overlooking money laundering and other suspicious customer payments that crisscrossed between the United States and countries such as Russia, Belarus and Mexico.

The illicit money was waved through even after securities regulators chided the bank two years ago over suspected money laundering and told it to be more vigilant.

Scores of transactions continued to cross easily as part of trillions of dollars of activity that the bank didn’t adequately monitor, the Treasury Department and the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency said in a joint statement announcing the fines.

Some of the transactions could be explained as “human error,” the Treasury Department said. Others demonstrated what regulators called systemic gaps in the bank’s compliance program, with Bank of America at times failing to make even cursory efforts to investigate suspicious activity.

Banks are required to file “suspicious activity reports” with the federal government when they believe transactions could be part of a money-laundering scheme, fraud or other illegal activity. Regulators said Bank of America had regularly avoided that, ignoring “large volumes of suspicious activity implicating national security-related risks,” including $600 million of transactions just involving salvaged vehicles.

It took Bank of America more than six months, in many instances, to file SARs — when it did so at all.

“Today’s actions send a clear message that even the biggest financial institutions are not above the law,” Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a statement.

Bank of America neither admitted nor denied the accusations. A spokeswoman, Christa Robinson, provided a statement that did not directly address the substance of the Treasury’s accusations but noted that the bank had worked with regulators to come to a resolution.

“We have invested billions of dollars in technology and dedicated thousands of employees to combat financial crime, and our team is far along with and committed to completing the work required to address the issues raised by our regulators,” Ms. Robinson said.

Bank of America is slated to report its quarterly earnings on Wednesday, and analysts expect that it earned about $8 billion in profit for the three-month period.

Last week, The New York Times published an analysis detailing how Russian companies evaded Western sanctions by funneling money through a Chinese bank with accounts at large Wall Street banks, including Bank of America.

The penalty on Tuesday was rare in both its size and its timing. Bank of America’s compliance with money-laundering laws was investigated under the Biden administration, but the Trump administration has taken a more relaxed approach to financial oversight. In recent weeks, however, regulators have been targeting banks on a range of issues.

Last week, the Federal Reserve and the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency fined American Express $350 million for failing to properly monitor billions of dollars of suspicious transactions that regulators said had spanned a decade.

Separately, Trump housing regulators said last week that they were investigating Wells Fargo over whether its lending efforts to encourage Black homeownership constituted racial discrimination.
